source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem
finding: Classic insight problems, non-insight problems and compound remote associates (CRAs) were compared on accuracy and self-reported Aha. Aha was higher for insight problems, but accuracy did not separate the types consistently.
numbers: Exp 1 N=184 analysed (193 recruited), Exp 1a N=74, Exp 2 N=117. Accuracy insight/non-insight/CRA: Exp1 .51/.54/.37; Exp1a .49/.64/.45; Exp2 .45/.56/.47. Aha-accuracy r: insight .50, CRA .41, non-insight .02 (Exp1); .40/.40/.24 (Exp1a); .495/.39/.19 (Exp2). Insight vs non-insight Aha diff 10.15 (Exp1).
limits: Student samples, 4 min per problem. One Aha cell in Exp 1a looks like a typo in the paper. Aha is self-report, so it cannot separate a distinct process from a feeling that goes with correct answers.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'insight problem' as proof of a special process. Route by observed solving behaviour, not by puzzle label.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem (process claim)
finding: The authors say their data cannot tell whether insight is a distinct solution process or a feeling that comes with correct solutions. Non-insight problems also showed an Aha-accuracy link, so they are not clean controls.
numbers: Multilevel logistic model best by BIC=5627.8: Pleasure beta 1.11, Impasse beta -1.08, Insight 0.51, Surprise -0.19 (predicting accuracy).
limits: Surprise related to Aha in all experiments but not to accuracy. Pooled native-English samples only.
agent_relevance: Feeling-of-certainty signals (pleasure, low impasse) track correctness; an agent could use a confidence-like signal but must check it against evidence.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha experience
finding: False insights exist. Wrong solutions to magic-trick problems also got strong Aha ratings, but correct solutions got stronger Aha, higher pleasure, suddenness and certainty, and came faster.
numbers: N=70 participants, 35 tricks, 2450 observations. 37% of incorrect solutions (417 of 1124) got Aha ratings above the mean for correct ones. Aha factors: Pleasure, Suddenness, Certainty; correct answers also showed Relief.
limits: Magic tricks only. Ratings given after solution, so hindsight may colour them.
agent_relevance: A strong 'got it' signal is not proof. Any agent rule that trusts a sudden confident answer needs an independent check (supports guardrails against over-trusting flashes).

source: Laukkonen et al. (2022) Eliciting false insights with semantic priming
finding: False insights were produced on purpose: priming with DRM-style lists plus visual similarity made people feel Aha for wrong anagram solutions. Experiment 2 replicated Experiment 1 and showed both factors were needed.
numbers: Total N=300 over 2 experiments. Primed lure anagrams M=0.37 false insights vs 0.07-0.09 for other anagram types, F(3,444)=171.52, d about 1.5-1.7. False insights weaker than correct ones: 5.81 vs 6.12, t(141)=2.57, d=-0.22. Intensity-accuracy r=.42. Exp 2: visual-similar anagrams with priming M=.24 vs scrambled .12; without priming .07 vs .09.
quote: Aha moments operate as a heuristic for deciding which ideas to trust.
limits: Anagrams only. Supports the view that Aha reflects past knowledge, so wrong knowledge gives wrong Aha.
agent_relevance: Misleading priming in context raises confident wrong answers. Matches LLM context-contamination risk: keep distractors out of the problem frame.

source: Macchi, Turco, Inglese & Caravona (2026) What pupil dilation reveals about unconscious analytic thought in insight problem solving
finding: Pupil size stayed high and flat during an incubation arithmetic task in people who later solved the insight problem, and fell in non-solvers and controls. The authors read this as unconscious analytic effort and use it in the dual-process debate.
numbers: N=91 recruited, 82 analysed: solvers n=11, non-solvers n=29, controls n=42. Significant group x time interaction on pupil size.
limits: Small solver group (n=11). Pupil size is also tied to arousal and task difficulty. Unconscious analytic thought is a contested reading, a rival to sudden Type 1 restructuring.
agent_relevance: Hints at background work during incubation. Weak support for a design where an agent keeps a pending problem alive while doing other steps.

source: Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis (J Intelligence 2023)
finding: Eye-movement traces on matchstick problems show abrupt representational change only when analysed with nonlinear models (GAMs, change points). ANOVA misses it. Explicit hints change the dynamics.
numbers: 61 participants in the sample described. Matchstick arithmetic insight and non-insight problems.
limits: Method paper. Whether change looks smooth or sudden depends on the statistics used, so some earlier null results for suddenness may be method artefacts.
agent_relevance: If insight is a sudden switch, an agent should look for discrete representation switches, not gradual drift.

source: Feelings-of-warmth increase more abruptly for verbal riddles solved with Aha (Frontiers Psychol 2018)
finding: The paper tests continuous vs discontinuous growth of the feeling of closeness (warmth) before solutions, with and without Aha, and whether Aha is stronger for self-solved than presented solutions. Title states warmth rises more abruptly with Aha.
numbers: Numbers not extracted (abstract and framing read only).
limits: Only the abstract and framing were read this session.
agent_relevance: Warmth jumps before Aha solutions: supports a sudden-switch signal, as in progress-monitoring accounts.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in LLMs using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT (Jan 2023) scored about like an average human on verbal insight problems. Authors suggest associative processes.
numbers: 30 verbal insight problems (Ansburg & Dominowski 2000). ChatGPT practice 7/15 (46.7%), transfer 5/15 (33.3%), pooled 12/30 (40%). Humans n=20: practice median .55, transfer .35.
limits: Small human sample, one model version, no contamination check.
agent_relevance: Early LLMs sit near human averages on classic insight items, but items may be memorised.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral thinking puzzles for LLMs
finding: On lateral-thinking puzzles that defeat the default commonsense association, models were far below humans and fragile under rewording.
numbers: Human 92% (3 experts, 102 sampled questions). ChatGPT 53% on sentence and 63% on word puzzles (original). Random 25%. About a third of models were at or below random. ChatGPT may have memorised some word puzzles (COW in thirteen letters).
limits: Multiple choice, not open generation. Group-based consistency across reconstructions much lower than single-item accuracy.
agent_relevance: Insight-like tasks expose pattern-completion failure. Rewording tests catch memorisation: use them to check any agent claim of insight.

source: Jiang, Ilievski & Ma (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9 BRAINTEASER
finding: Top systems reached 100% on both subtasks after fine-tuning or prompting, but most models dropped on semantic and context reconstructions.
numbers: Human .920; ChatGPT baseline .627 overall; RoBERTa-L .434. 48 team submissions (sentence puzzles), 37 (word puzzles). Over 80% of models fell on original+semantic grouping, by 0.025 to 0.175 (SP) and 0.031 to 0.281 (WP). Drops on all three variants: 0.025-0.275 (SP), 0.031-0.344 (WP). 90% of prompting teams used closed LLMs such as GPT-4.
limits: Authors say lateral thinking is not solved; 100% scores come with fine-tuning on in-distribution data.
agent_relevance: Instance accuracy overstates ability. Use group-based consistency when scoring an agent on insight-like items.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in LLMs (Study 1: CRT)
finding: Early GPT-3 models answered like humans do on the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT), taking the intuitive trap. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly avoided it.
numbers: 150 generated CRT tasks. Humans: 38% correct (original study 41%, n=3,428), 55% intuitive. GPT-3-davinci-003: 5% correct, 80% intuitive. ChatGPT-3.5: 59% correct, 15% intuitive. ChatGPT-4: 96% correct, 0% intuitive.
limits: CRT is math-heavy. Newer models may have seen CRT items. Their human sample differs from lab samples.
agent_relevance: Type 1 trap behaviour in LLMs shrinks with scale; do not assume an LLM has an exploitable 'intuition' stage.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Studies 2 and 3: chain of thought and few-shot
finding: Chain of thought (CoT) lifted GPT-3 correct answers and cut intuitive ones. Blocking CoT in ChatGPT kept most gains, so the models have learned System-1-like correctness. A few worked examples taught GPT-3 the trick.
numbers: Study 2: GPT-3-davinci-003 with CoT correct 5%->28%, intuitive 80%->29%. Blocking CoT: ChatGPT-3.5 CoT 97%->0%, correct unchanged (p=.49); ChatGPT-4 correct 95%->88%, intuitive 0%->10%. Study 3: accuracy 2%->92% after two examples (Type 2), 12%->92% after seven (Type 3), 0%->78% after 30 examples (Type 1 hardest).
limits: ChatGPT-4 solved 24% of CRT without CoT in Study 1. Item generation is automatic and uniform.
agent_relevance: Few examples can shift an LLM from trap to correct. A scaffold that adds a reflective check pays most for small or older models.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Studies 4 and 5: semantic illusions
finding: On semantic illusions, which need no math, GPT-3 fell for the trap 72% of the time. ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were correct 74% and 88%. Reflection instructions and examples raised accuracy.
numbers: Atypical answers fell 52% (babbage) to 10% (davinci-003). Correct: 18% (davinci-003), 74% (ChatGPT-3.5), 88% (ChatGPT-4). With prompting, correct rose 18%->54% and intuitive 72%->28%; 18%->64% after 10 or more examples. Human baseline: 64% intuitive vs 52% in original (n=61).
limits: Task-specific prompts. Human baseline from one online sample.
agent_relevance: Confirms the trap-then-correct shape generalises beyond arithmetic.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: Abstract-level: GPT-3 does vignette tasks as well as or better than people, but small perturbations send it wrong, and it fails a causal reasoning task.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract page only).
limits: Abstract only. Did not read the CRT or heuristics sections.
agent_relevance: Perturbation test is the right check for shallow success on classic tasks.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-like training: a critical perspective
finding: The 'aha moment' of self-reflection in R1-Zero was already present in base models including DeepSeek-V3-Base. In R1-Zero, self-reflection did not reliably raise accuracy.
numbers: 500 MATH questions with R1 template; 8 samples each. Self-reflection keywords ('recheck', 'wait', 'Aha') appear in DeepSeek-V3-Base. Fig 15: for DeepSeek-R1-Zero, nearly half of responses with self-reflection were not more accurate than those without (100 samples per question). Qwen2.5-Math without template gains about 60% over 4-shot on 5 benchmarks.
limits: Keyword and LLM-judged detection of reflection can mislabel. Math benchmarks, not insight puzzles.
agent_relevance: Reflection tokens are not an insight mechanism. Do not count 'wait' as evidence of restructuring.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (aha moment, Table 2)
finding: Authors describe an intermediate DeepSeek-R1-Zero that stops, says 'Wait, wait. Wait. That's an aha moment I can flag here', and rethinks. They count it as emergent reasoning from RL.
numbers: Table 2 example only; no frequency count of such moments in the text read.
quote: That's an aha moment I can flag here.
limits: Anecdote chosen by authors. Later work (the Liu et al. line above) found similar behaviour in the base model.
agent_relevance: The 'aha' language is a style RL rewards or base models already hold; treat as a prompt cue (O4/O6), not proof of insight.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: agent with fast and slow thinking
finding: A dual-process agent (fast small model for routine action, slow LLM for planning and subgoals) beat single-process LLM agents on ScienceWorld. It tests a dual-process architecture directly.
numbers: 30 ScienceWorld task types. Average score: SwiftSage 84.7, Reflexion 45.3, ReAct 36.4, SayCan 33.8.
limits: Needs an environment-based fast module. The 'fast' side is behaviour cloning, not human-style intuition. Mapping to insight theory is loose.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct AI test of dual-process design. Supports a fast default with a slow fallback trigger; matches S0-S9 style switching.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention
finding: Rewriting the context first to strip opinions and distractors (a selective-encoding step) raised accuracy and reduced sycophancy.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat. Factuality on opinion-laden TriviaQA 62.8%->80.3% (200 prompts). GSM-IC math with irrelevant sentences 51.7%->61.3% (100 problems). Objectivity on longform arguments +57.4% as reported.
limits: Extra inference pass. Judged by GPT-4 for factuality. One model family.
agent_relevance: Closest AI match to Sternberg's selective encoding. Filtering the input before reasoning gives measured gains.

source: Davidson & Sternberg (1984) The role of insight in intellectual giftedness
finding: Founding study: gifted children did better on insight problems and benefitted more from help with selective encoding, selective combination and selective comparison. The three-process theory says insight is a skilled use of these processes, not a special mechanism.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled from memory, not opened this session; numbers not verified. Exact N and effect sizes unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Process names give a checklist: filter relevant facts, combine them, compare to old knowledge (maps to O4, O6).

source: Davidson (1995, 2003) The suddenness of insight; Insights about insightful problem solving
finding: Davidson's review says the three processes need not be sudden or unconscious. The sudden Aha is a result of a good selective step plus a restructuring that follows from it.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled from memory, not opened this session; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Do not make the scaffold depend on a sudden-switch event.

source: Weisberg (2014/2015) Toward an integrated theory of insight; Fleck & Weisberg (2004, 2013) Insight versus analysis
finding: Verbal protocol studies find a large share of solutions to classic insight problems come by plain analysis, with only some showing Aha. Argues for one set of ordinary processes with different outcomes.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled from memory, not opened this session; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Supports using normal search with restructuring, not a separate insight mode.

source: Gilhooly & Murphy (2005) Differentiating insight from non-insight problems
finding: Cluster analysis of problem types gave only partial support for a clean split between insight and non-insight problems.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled from memory, not opened this session; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Problem labels are blunt tools for routing.

source: Chuderski & Jastrzebski (2018) Much ado about aha: insight problem solving is strongly related to working memory capacity and reasoning ability
finding: Title (seen in Crossref and Europe PMC listings, full text not accessed) says insight problem solving is strongly related to working memory capacity and reasoning ability, against a separate insight ability.
numbers: Not verified. Title only.
limits: Title and venue seen; contents not read.
agent_relevance: Suggests capacity, not a special insight faculty, drives performance: more budget helps.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden & Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions
finding: Cited by Webb 2016 and Laukkonen 2022 for the finding that Aha solutions are more often correct than non-Aha solutions.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Recalled from memory, not opened this session; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Aha as accuracy signal; partly contradicted by false-insight work (b03, b04).

source: Evaluating the cognitive reflection test as a measure of intuition/reflection, numeracy, and insight problem solving (J Exp Psychol Gen 2019)
finding: Title (Europe PMC listing) says the CRT relates to numeracy and insight problem solving, so it is not a pure reflection measure.
numbers: Not verified. Title only.
limits: Author list not recorded; contents not read.
agent_relevance: Hagendorff CRT results may mix numeracy and insight-like trap detection.

source: Oat-Zero blog (2025): There may not be an aha moment in R1-Zero-like training
finding: Cited in Liu et al. 2025 as finding self-reflection keywords in open R1 replication base models already.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: Same warning: reflection tokens predate RL.
